summary: Specifies a multipath extension for OLSRv2 to find several disjoint paths in mobile ad hoc networks. Multiple paths can improve throughput and reliability by avoiding single route failures. It stays interoperable with OLSRv2 and is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: If one road breaks, a second road is ready. This helps wireless gadgets that move around find extra routes.

questions: how does multipath dijkstra algorithm work
subtitle: Multiple disjoint paths for reliable routing in mobile ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc networks need to deliver data reliably when the topology changes constantly and single routes can fail.
tldr.mechanism: MP-OLSRv2 extends the OLSRv2 routing protocol to find multiple disjoint paths to each destination using a Multipath Dijkstra Algorithm, then forwards datagrams using source routing to distribute traffic across the paths.
tldr.outcome: Multiple paths increase aggregated throughput, improve reliability against route failures, and enable load balancing in dynamic networks. The extension stays interoperable with standard OLSRv2.

today: RFC 8218 is Experimental. It extends RFC 7181 (OLSRv2) for mobile ad hoc networks and has not been obsoleted. Implementations are encouraged to test it and report experience to advance the protocol toward Standards Track.

sections.title: Why Multiple Paths in Mobile Networks
sections.content:
OLSRv2 is a routing protocol designed for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs), where devices move around and connections change constantly. Like a traditional routing protocol, OLSRv2 finds one shortest path to each destination.

Multipath OLSRv2 (MP-OLSRv2) extends this to discover multiple disjoint paths to the same destination. Because paths do not share many routers or links, if one path fails due to topology changes, traffic can use another. This improves both reliability and throughput: devices can send data on multiple paths at once to increase speed, or switch paths if one breaks without losing connection.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a package, instead of betting on one road, the router picks two or three different roads to use. If a road closes, the package already has a backup.

sections.title: How MP-OLSRv2 Works
sections.content:
MP-OLSRv2 builds on OLSRv2 by adding three main pieces. First, it identifies routers that support source routing—the ability to follow a path explicitly named in the packet header—by adding a SOURCE_ROUTE flag to HELLO and Topology Control (TC) messages. Only routers that advertise this flag can be placed in a source route.

Second, it maintains a Multipath Routing Set, a table of multiple paths to each destination. This can be calculated proactively (before packets need to go) or reactively (on demand when a packet arrives). Each path stores the list of intermediate routers and a metric for path quality.

Third, when a datagram leaves, the originating router applies the Multipath Dijkstra Algorithm to select up to NUMBER_OF_PATHS different paths, picks one based on a scheduler (round-robin or per-flow), and embeds that path in the packet header using source routing. Intermediate routers forward the packet to the next hop named in the header.
sections.plainLanguage: The router marks which routers can handle source routes. It keeps a list of multiple paths to each destination. When sending a package, it picks a path, writes the list of stops on the envelope, and sends it. Each router reads where to go next.

sections.title: Messages and Packet Headers
sections.content:
HELLO and TC messages use the standard OLSRv2 format, with one addition: a SOURCE_ROUTE Type-Length-Value (TLV) field that signals the originating router supports source-route forwarding. This flag allows receivers to identify which routers are safe to put in a source route.

Datagrams carry source routing headers specific to the IP version. In IPv4, an optional loose source routing header lists the IP addresses to visit; routers between listed addresses can forward the packet freely. In IPv6, a strict source routing header (defined in RFC 6554 as Routing Type 3) lists all intermediate routers that must be visited in exact order. Source route information occupies space in the packet header, so for long paths the implementation may select only "key" routers (for example, uniformly spaced ones) to stay within the maximum header size.
sections.plainLanguage: HELLO and TC messages add a small flag saying 'I can do source routing.' Packets carry a list of routers to visit, either loosely (IPv4, some hops can be skipped) or strictly (IPv6, all hops must be exact).

sections.title: The Multipath Dijkstra Algorithm
sections.content:
To find multiple disjoint paths without always choosing inferior ones, MP-OLSRv2 uses the Multipath Dijkstra Algorithm. It runs Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly; after finding each path, it increases the metric (cost) of links and edges used in that path to discourage the next iteration from reusing them, then reruns Dijkstra to find a different path.

The algorithm applies two metric-increase functions. The fp function (default fp(c) = 4*c) increases the metric of links that are part of the previous path, encouraging the next path to use different links. The fe function (default fe(c) = 2*c) increases the metric of links that touch intermediate routers of the previous path. By choosing fp > fe, the algorithm prefers to share nodes rather than links, reducing the chance of choosing very inferior paths. The result is paths that are disjoint enough to avoid a single failure but not so strict that a bottleneck forces a much longer detour.

The calculation requires the CUTOFF_RATIO parameter: if a path's metric exceeds CUTOFF_RATIO * best_metric (default ratio 1.5), the path is discarded as too poor. NUMBER_OF_PATHS (default 3) sets how many paths to keep.
sections.plainLanguage: Run the shortest-path algorithm once, then increase the cost of roads you just used. Run it again to find a different path, then increase those roads. Repeat until you have enough paths. Throw away any path that is way too long.

sections.title: Deployment and Status
sections.content:
MP-OLSRv2 is published as Experimental, meaning the IETF encourages implementation and testing but expects the protocol to evolve. The specification documents open questions: optimal values for the number of paths, the right metric functions for link-disjoint versus node-disjoint paths, the impact of OLSRv2's partial topology knowledge on path quality, and how multipath routing interacts with transport protocols sensitive to reordering (like TCP) versus those that tolerate it (like UDP with erasure coding for video).

In a router, MP-OLSRv2 does not have to replace OLSRv2 entirely. Operators can apply multipath routing selectively to certain applications (identified by a Diffserv codepoint) that benefit from it, while leaving others on standard OLSRv2. Mixed networks with both MP-OLSRv2 and OLSRv2-only routers can coexist: MP-OLSRv2 uses loose source routing in IPv4 to interoperate with routers that do not understand source routes, and in IPv6 it excludes non-source-routing routers from paths.

Security depends on the underlying OLSRv2 integrity and replay protection (RFC 7183). A new threat is source-routing attacks: a compromised router could forge a SOURCE_ROUTE flag and be placed in critical paths, or receive misdirected traffic. Implementations must drop datagrams with source routing headers at the boundary of the routing domain.
sections.plainLanguage: This is still experimental, so networks try it and send feedback. A router can use it for some traffic and OLSRv2 for other traffic. Mixed networks with old routers work because MP-OLSRv2 can skip old routers or work around them. You need to protect the system so bad routers can't fake a source-routing capability.
